props.title: Coming Home
props.initialSlug: Vietnam vet finds love while healing war's wounds

sections.content: Coming Home (1978) represents a pivotal shift in how Hollywood portrayed Vietnam veterans, delivering raw emotional truth instead of exploitation. Hal Ashby directs Jane Fonda and Jon Voight in a love triangle that confronts PTSD, disability, and societal reintegration head-on. The film arrived alongside The Deer Hunter (1978), marking 1978 as the year mainstream cinema finally processed Vietnam's psychological toll. Unlike the violent spectacle of later films like Rambo: First Blood (1982), Coming Home emphasizes intimate human drama and healing.

sections.content: Hal Ashby's humanist direction in Coming Home builds on his earlier character studies like Harold and Maude (1971) and The Last Detail (1973). The film's soundtrack revolutionized how pop music could drive emotional resonance, with Beatles and Rolling Stones tracks amplifying key moments. This influenced later Vietnam films like Apocalypse Now (1979) and Full Metal Jacket (1987) to use period-specific music as psychological commentary.

Jane Fonda's Sally Hyde marks a crucial evolution in how films depicted military spouses, moving beyond simplistic "waiting wife" stereotypes. Her sexual awakening with Voight's paralyzed vet Luke Martin challenged mainstream cinema's treatment of disability and intimacy. This groundbreaking portrayal influenced later films like The Sessions (2012) and Rust and Bone (2012). SUBHEAD: Impact on Vietnam War Cinema

sections.content: Coming Home launched a wave of serious Vietnam examinations that peaked with Platoon (1986) and Good Morning, Vietnam (1987). These films finally allowed America to process the war's complexity through art rather than propaganda. The authentic portrayal of veterans' struggles influenced later PTSD-focused films like In the Valley of Elah (2007) and Brothers (2009).
